title: Finding the PHP versions in your repos that need the php2shell fix
partialText:
php.net shipped the fixes for php2shell (CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619) on 21 Oct. To patch, you need a list of every PHP you run, and the versions written in your repos mostly can’t give you one. Across 10 public repos, 112 PHP version declarations were labeled before running the tool, and 111 of them can’t prove which PHP build actually runs.

So the work splits in two: find every place a repo declares PHP, then work out which ones you can fix by changing a line and which ones you have to check on a real build.

The fixed versions, and a 60-second check

From php.net’s advisory:

8.1 and older get no official release. php.net published source backport branches for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 ( PHP-8.1-CVE-2026-109618-109619 in php-src, and the same pattern for the other two), and some distros and LTS vendors backport.

The advisory puts the highest risk on installs that serve web requests: PHP-FPM and mod_php first, then php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. CI runners and dev machines still need the update. They’re just less exposed. If you can’t update yet, the advisory lists mitigations. php.net says they reduce exposure and don’t fix the bug, so I’m linking them instead of copying them here.

To see what a host or image actually runs:

For official images and source builds, PHP_VERSION is the answer. For distro packages it isn't. Debian, Ubuntu and RHEL backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so compare the package version with your vendor's security tracker. If you install from Remi's repo, it had no updates as of 21 Oct.

Where PHP versions hide in a repo

That check needs a list of hosts and images to run it on, and the repo is where that list comes from. Each place PHP shows up says something different about the build.

Exact official tags. FROM php:8.3.30-fpm is as close to proof as a repo gets. The docker-library images are built from source at that version, so anything built from this line runs 8.3.30. Whether that's the image you deployed is a separate question.

Floating tags. FROM php:8.3-fpm resolves at build time. You get the fix once the official image is rebuilt on 8.3.36 and you rebuild with --pull and redeploy. Restarting the same container keeps the old build, and so does reusing a tag with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.

setup-php. php-version: '8.3.30' looks like a pin. setup-php installs whatever 8.3 patch is current or already on the runner, so a version at or above the fix can still run an older build. The first draft of the tool's spec treated these as exact pins. The tool treats them as floating.

Version files. asdf installs exactly what .tool-versions says, so php 8.4.20 there is a real pin. .php-version is different: setup-php, Symfony CLI and Herd read it and use whatever patch is installed.

Distro packages. apt-get install php8.2-cli gets you whatever the vendor ships, and the version string won't show a backported fix.

Images that bundle PHP. wordpress, drupal, nextcloud and Laravel Sail runtimes have PHP inside and no PHP version on the FROM line. The fix arrives when the maintainer rebuilds and you pull.

Composer constraints. "php": "^8.2" tells Composer what the code supports. It doesn't pick the runtime. Updating Laravel, Symfony or WordPress code doesn't change the runtime either, since php2shell is in PHP itself.

EOL branches. 8.1 and older need action however they’re declared: upgrade, take a vendor backport, or build from php.net’s backport branch.

What I measured

The corpus is 10 public PHP repos, each pinned to a commit SHA. The labels were made by reading each repo’s files line by line before running the tool on it, with an AI coding assistant, in one labeling pass. They’re recorded in results/labels.json, line level. Recall only covers the file types the labeling grep covered: Dockerfiles, Containerfiles, YAML, .php-version, .tool-versions and composer.json. The baseline is grep -rnE "FROM +php:", the usual "inventory your Dockerfiles" step. I'm not publishing per-repo verdicts.

Six repos were the tuning set. On the first run the tool found 58 of 69 labeled declarations, with 3 false positives, and grep found 31. The miss worth knowing about even if you never run the tool: setup-php versions that aren’t written next to setup-php. Some were set under env: and read back as ${{ env.php-version }}, and some were passed as an input to a reusable workflow ( with: php-versions: "['8.3', '8.4']"). Search a workflow for setup-php and you'll find the step, but the version lives somewhere else.

After fixing those gaps, the tuning set went to 70 of 70. That’s tuned on the same repos, so it doesn’t count. (It’s 70 now because the labeling pass missed one declaration, which was added after the first run.) Then 4 more repos were labeled the same way and measured once:

The 6 held-out misses were setup-php referenced by full URL ( uses: https://github.com/shivammathur/setup-php@v2, common on Forgejo), an Arch pacman -S install, and Debian's libapache2-mod-php. That last one is mod_php, one of the two highest-risk setups in the advisory, and its package name doesn't start with php. All 6 are fixed in the release, so 36 of 42 measures the code from before those fixes.

Across all 10 repos, 111 of the 112 labeled declarations can’t prove which PHP build runs: floating tags, setup-php, distro packages, Sail runtimes, bundled images, templated tags and composer constraints. The one exception is a .tool-versions file with a patch version. Against php.net's fix table, a naive version compare gives a firm "vulnerable" or "fixed" on all 95 version-dependent, non-EOL findings whose source can't prove the runtime. Each of those is a guess.

It’s a small corpus with one labeling pass. Every run is in results/runs/, with the method in results/numbers.md.

The tool

php2shell-repo-audit reads those files and puts each declaration in ACTION REQUIRED, CHECK MANUALLY or DECLARED ≥ FIXED, with a reason. It never calls a repo fine: DECLARED ≥ FIXED always means “runtime not verified”. It needs Node 20 or newer and has no runtime dependencies.

--org reads default branches with a token from GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or gh auth token, GET requests only, and skips archived repos and forks. It only sees what the token can read, so check the repo count it prints.

Here’s the published 0.1.0 on the demo repo, which is synthetic: a made-up repo with 7 planted declarations.

$ npx php2shell-repo-audit@0.1.0 demo-repo php2shell-repo-audit 0.1.0 · fix table rev 2: published 2026-10-21, https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5 (remote) Reads PHP versions declared in this repo. It does not check running servers. ACTION REQUIRED (3) .tool-versions:2 dev php 8.4.20 vulnerable: fixed in 8.4.27, upgrade docker/api/Dockerfile:1 prod FROM php:8.3.30-fpm vulnerable: fixed in 8.3.36, upgrade docker/legacy/Dockerfile:1 prod FROM php:8.1-fpm eol: no official php.net release for 8.1; upgrade, use your vendor's backport, or build from php.net's backport branch PHP-8.1-CVE-2026-109618-109619 CHECK MANUALLY (4) .github/workflows/ci.yml:10 ci setup-php 8.3 floating-rebuild: setup-php installs the current or pre-installed 8.3 patch, not a pinned build Dockerfile:1 prod FROM php:8.3-fpm floating-rebuild: rebuild with --pull and redeploy after the release, then confirm with the docker run check composer.json:6 prod "php": "^8.2" constraint-only: a composer constraint is not the runtime docker/worker/Dockerfile:3 prod apt-get install php8.2-cli distro-vendor: vendors backport fixes without changing the version; check your vendor's security tracker DECLARED ≥ FIXED (0) The docker run check: docker run --rm --entrypoint php <image> -r 'echo PHP_VERSION;' exit 1: action required

grep finds 3 of those 7 lines. The two exact pins below the fix and the 8.1 image get a firm verdict. Everything the repo can’t settle goes to CHECK MANUALLY with the thing to check.

As a GitHub Action:

It writes the findings to the job summary. By default it fails on ACTION REQUIRED, on anything that needs a manual check, and when it finds no PHP at all. A green job means nothing this repo declares needs attention, and says nothing about the runtime.

What it doesn’t see

It reads git. That leaves out:

  • Servers and shared hosting that aren’t described in a repo: cPanel, Plesk, .htaccess PHP handlers.
  • PaaS and managed runtimes such as Platform.sh, Upsun, Laravel Vapor, Bref, Forge and Heroku. The README has the full list.
  • Helm and Kustomize templates, compose extends:, GitLab include:, and versions set in .env files.
  • The image you actually deployed, and anything built outside the repo. That’s what the docker run line is for.
  • With --org, anything that isn't on a default branch. A service built from another branch or an old tag won't be in the list.

The next thing I’d build is an inspect <image> command that runs php inside an image and checks its distro packages, so CI can check the build instead of the file that describes it. Until that exists, the repo gives you the list of things to rebuild, and the docker run line is still the only step here that looks at a real build.

Originally published at https://amsozzer.com on October 21, 2026.

Finding the PHP versions in your repos that need the php2shell fix was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Two iOS Modals, One View Controller: The Bug That Blocked New Currencies in My Budget App
partialText:
On iOS, the "+ Add” currency button in my budget app did nothing at all. The cause was a React Native modal asking UIKit for something it refuses to do, and the fix is a rule worth knowing if your app stacks modals.

TL;DR — In Noma, the free offline budget tracker I build for people living across currencies, the “+ Add” button that adds a new currency from the expense sheet shipped dead on iOS and survived a few releases. The app’s modals were rendered as siblings, and on iOS each React Native Modal is a view controller presented from its host's nearest controller, which was already busy presenting the expense sheet. UIKit refused the second present and logged a warning that never reaches production error tracking. The fix renders a stacked modal inside its opener, and makes a modal that replaces its opener wait for onDismiss on iOS.

Here’s the Situation

The “+ Add” button in Noma’s expense sheet did nothing on iOS, and it shipped that way for a few releases.

In Noma you set a main currency once, during onboarding, and every amount you record gets converted to it. On top of that you track the other currencies you spend in, and you can add a new one whenever you need it.

Outside onboarding, that happens in two places: the entry sheet you open with “+” on a category card, and the income modal. Take an expense: you type the amount, and below it sits a row of currency pills with a dashed “+ Add” at the end. Tap it, type a code like PLN, and the new currency is ready for this expense and every one after it.

That was the bug: on iOS, the expense sheet just stayed where it was after the tap, with no error and no crash.

For most of those releases, a Playwright test in CI tapped this exact button and kept passing. I’ll get to why.

An automated screen-capture run caught it. On 2026–10–20 it ran on an iOS 26.4 simulator with preview build 1.1.78 and failed the transactions flow in every theme pass. The step that tapped “+ Add” completed, and the next step, waiting for the currency code field, failed. The same flow passed on Android.

What It Breaks for a Nomad

This dead button sat on the path a nomad hits the first time a trip takes them into a new currency. With “+ Add” dead on iOS, the options left are all bad:

  • Log the expense in a currency you already track and convert it in your head. Noma stores every expense with the exchange rate at the moment you record it, so a hand conversion freezes your guess into the history.
  • Skip it and log it later. Later is where small expenses go to be forgotten, and a week of forgotten ones is how a travel budget drifts without anyone noticing.
  • Run onboarding again from Settings > My Data, which can add tracked currencies. That path works on iOS, because the onboarding screen opens Add currency on its own, with no other modal underneath. But it’s a strange detour for one expense, and it’s blocked entirely while your phone is paired with a partner through couple sync.

For a multi-currency budget, adding a currency is core behavior. When it breaks, every entry in the new currency ends up either wrong or missing.

The Warning Nobody Reads

The simulator log had the whole story in one line:

[com.apple.UIKit:Presentation] Attempt to present <RCTFabricModalHostViewController: 0x12a04e300>
on <UIViewController: 0x1045fdc00> (from <RNSScreen: 0x10460c000>)
which is already presenting <RCTFabricModalHostViewController: 0x12a04c500>.

That is UIKit saying no. Because it is a log line and not an exception, nothing reaches crash reporting or the JavaScript console, and the tap simply has no effect.

The end-to-end suite didn’t see it either. A Playwright test opens an expense sheet, types 50, taps “+ Add” and expects the Add currency sheet to open. It runs in desktop Chrome against the app’s web build, where a React Native modal is a layer in the DOM, and two layers stack without asking any view controller. So the test kept passing while the same tap did nothing on iOS.

How the Modals Were Wired

Most of the app’s modals, including the transaction, income, add-currency and add-group modals, lived in one place: a TabBarAndModals component at the root of the tab navigator, which rendered them as siblings in one fragment. They go through the same building blocks, a ModalShell that wraps a Dialog, which renders its own React Native <Modal>.

This is what the relevant part looked like before the fix, with props trimmed:

// apps/mobile/app/(tabs)/_layout.tsx (before the fix)
<TransactionModal
  isOpen={modals.transaction.isOpen}
  onClose={() => closeModal('transaction')}
  currencies={currencies}
  onSubmit={handleTransactionSubmit}
  onAddCurrency={() => openModal('currency')}
/>
 
{/* ...other modals... */}
 
<AddCurrencyModal
  key={`add-currency-${modals.currency.isOpen}`}
  isOpen={modals.currency.isOpen}
  onClose={() => closeModal('currency')}
  onAdd={handleAddCurrency}
  existingCurrencies={currencies}
/>

The “+ Add” pill calls onAddCurrency, which calls openModal('currency') from a small modal manager hook:

// packages/hooks/src/hooks/use-modal-manager.ts
const openModal = useCallback(
  <T extends ModalName>(name: T, data?: ModalDataMap[T]) => {
    setModals((prev) => ({
      ...prev,
      [name]: { ...prev[name], isOpen: true, ...(data ?? {}) },
    }));
  },
  [],
);

It flips one flag. The transaction modal stays open underneath, which is exactly what you want: after adding a currency you should land back on your half-typed expense.

On Android this works. On iOS it can’t.

Why iOS Refuses and Android Doesn’t

On iOS, a React Native <Modal> is a real view controller, and React Native presents it from the nearest view controller of the modal's host view.

Both modals here are siblings, so both hosts resolve to the same view controller. When the transaction sheet opens, that controller presents it. When “+ Add” flips the currency flag, React Native asks the same controller to present a second one. A UIKit view controller presents one thing at a time, so it refuses and logs the warning above.

Android draws a React Native modal as a dialog window. Two dialogs can stack without any parent and child relationship, which is why the same code passed there.

There’s a nasty detail after the refusal. As far as React knows, the currency modal is open: modals.currency.isOpen is true. A second tap on "+ Add" sets it to true again, which changes nothing, so the button should stay dead until the app restarts. I haven't checked that part on a device.

Every Place One Modal Opens Another

Once the mechanism was clear, the bug turned into a pattern to hunt. I traced every place in the app where one React Native modal opens another, and had each site checked by two independent reviewers.

The last row is a variant. “Create Savings group” closed investment settings and opened the Create group modal in the same batch, so the second present ran while the first sheet was still animating out. Same refusal, different timing.

A few things worth noting about what was not affected. Modals opened from inside another modal’s tree were fine, like editing a transaction from a category’s history, or the select sheets inside dialogs. The system share sheet was fine too, because it presents from the topmost view controller.

The wiring went back to the app’s early single-screen layout, before the iOS launch, and the income modal joined the list later.

The Fix: Two Rules for Stacked Modals on iOS

The fix comes down to two rules, now written into the mobile app’s docs next to the modal building blocks.

Rule 1: a modal that stacks on top of its opener renders inside the opener.

ModalShell got a stackedModal slot. Whatever you pass there renders inside its Dialog, after the content, so on iOS it presents from the opener's own view controller instead of the busy parent:

// apps/mobile/components/ui/modal-shell.tsx
return (
  <Dialog open={isOpen} onOpenChange={handleOpenChange} onDismiss={onDismiss}>
    <DialogContent testID={testID} backdropDismiss={dismiss !== 'explicit'}>
      {/* header and children */}
    </DialogContent>
    {stackedModal}
  </Dialog>
);

It sits after DialogContent on purpose, outside the sheet's ScrollView: a modal mounted under a ScrollView loses its first tap to that ScrollView, which dismisses the keyboard instead of pressing the button.

The layout now builds the add-currency modal once and hands it to both openers:

// apps/mobile/app/(tabs)/_layout.tsx
const addCurrencyModal = (
  <AddCurrencyModal
    key={`add-currency-${modals.currency.isOpen}`}
    isOpen={modals.currency.isOpen}
    onClose={() => closeModal('currency')}
    onAdd={handleAddCurrency}
    existingCurrencies={currencies}
  />
);
 
<TransactionModal
  // ...
  onAddCurrency={() => openModal('currency')}
  addCurrencyModal={addCurrencyModal}
/>

The fix leaves the modal state alone, since openModal('currency') still flips the same flag, and moves only the modal's place in the tree, which on iOS decides which controller presents it.

This is the same shape the app already used where things worked, like editing a transaction from a category’s history: the child modal lived inside the parent’s tree all along.

Rule 2: a modal that replaces its opener waits for onDismiss on iOS.

Investment settings doesn’t need to stay open under the new group form, so stacking would be wrong there. The opener has to go away first. Dialog and ModalShell now forward onDismiss to React Native's Modal, and the settings modal uses it:

// apps/mobile/components/modals/investment-settings-modal.tsx
const createAfterDismissRef = useRef(false);
 
const handleCreateSavingsGroup = () => {
  onClose();
  if (Platform.OS === 'ios') {
    createAfterDismissRef.current = true;
 
    return;
  }
  onCreateSavingsGroup();
};
 
const handleDismiss = () => {
  if (!createAfterDismissRef.current) {
    return;
  }
  createAfterDismissRef.current = false;
  onCreateSavingsGroup();
};

React Native fires onDismiss on iOS only, so Android keeps opening the group form right away. On iOS the form now appears about 0.3 seconds after the settings sheet fades out. Before the fix, it never appeared. The ref guard matters too: a plain dismissal, where the user just closes settings, opens nothing.

Tests that fail on the old code

Each new assertion fails on the code before the fix and passes after it:

  • the add-currency modal renders inside the transaction modal’s Modal, and inside the income modal's;
  • the stacked modal has no ScrollView ancestor;
  • on iOS, “Create Savings group” closes the settings modal, waits for onDismiss, requests the group once, and requests nothing on a plain dismissal;
  • on Android it requests the group right away.

A unit test can’t prove UIKit’s behavior, but it can pin the tree shape and the dismiss-then-open order that keep UIKit happy.

After the Fix

A later capture run, on build 1.1.80, which carries the fix, walked the same flow on iOS and got the shot the first run kept failing on:

The fix is merged and ships to the stores with the next release. Until then, iOS users on older builds still have the onboarding detour.

What I Learned

On iOS, a React Native modal is a view controller presentation. Where it sits in the tree decides which view controller presents it. Two sibling modals compete for the same presenter, and the second one loses.

A refused present fails silently. UIKit logs a warning and moves on, so no exception reaches your error tracking, and the only signal is a button that does nothing. Unit tests and a Playwright run on the web build both work with no UIKit underneath, so neither can see this kind of refusal. Flows that stack modals are worth an end-to-end run on a real iOS runtime.

Rare paths need the same care as daily ones. Adding a currency after onboarding is rare for someone who stays put. For a nomad it happens every time a trip leads into a currency the budget doesn’t track yet, and that is exactly when the budget matters most.

Write the rule down next to the building blocks. The fix took two small changes. Keeping it fixed takes a rule the next modal will follow: stacked modals render inside their opener, and replacing modals wait for onDismiss on iOS.

Final Thoughts

The bug was a few lines of tree placement. It survived a few releases and a green end-to-end test, and its effect landed on the one moment a multi-currency budget has to get right: the first expense in a new currency. A budget is only as honest as the entries in it, and an entry you couldn’t log in the right currency is either a guess or a gap.

The habit that keeps a travel budget accurate is logging each expense when you pay, in the currency you paid. The app’s job is to make that one tap work every time, on both platforms.

If you track money across currencies, Noma is on iOS and Android:

  • Website: https://getnoma.pro
  • App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6762905387
  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=pro.getnoma.app

Have you hit a silent UIKit refusal in React Native? I’d like to hear which modal it was and how you found it.

I hope this was helpful. Good luck, and happy engineering!
